paths.title: Start Here
paths.subtitle: The essentials, one record at a time, in order
paths.intro: Fourteen records, one from each turn the music took, in the order it took them. Play each one through before moving on; by the end you'll have heard the whole story, from the blues queens to last decade.
paths.outro: From here, follow whatever caught your ear: every record's page has three doors out of it.

paths.title: Jazz for People Who Think They Hate Jazz
paths.subtitle: Melody, groove and short tracks first
paths.intro: If jazz has ever sounded to you like noodling, start here: tunes you can hum, grooves you can move to, nothing over seven minutes. Every one of them was a hit with people who didn't think they liked jazz either.

stops.note: Five beats to the bar, but it never feels odd: a piano vamp that won't let go and a saxophone melody that floats over it. It sold a million copies.
A boogaloo groove and a trumpet line you'll be humming tomorrow. Listen to how the drums and bass lock in before the horns arrive.
Four chords, round and round. The fun is hearing each soloist find something new to say over the same few bars.

stops.track: Stan Getz & João Gilberto|The Girl from Ipanema|1963
stops.note: Bossa nova: a soft guitar rhythm, a whispered voice, a saxophone that never raises itself. Jazz at its gentlest.
A Brazilian-tinged bass line under a melody built from one simple phrase. Steely Dan borrowed the opening for Rikki Don't Lose That Number.
Joe Zawinul's slow gospel groove, recorded live: listen to the crowd. It reached the pop charts in 1967.
Funk, synthesizers and a bass line that walks into the room: the best-selling jazz album of its time.
Jazz musicians playing R&B and hip-hop as if there were no line between them, with Erykah Badu singing a 1959 jazz standard.

paths.outro: If one of these grabbed you, its album page has three more doors. If you liked the grooves, try The Latin Tinge.

paths.subtitle: The year jazz went five directions at once
paths.intro: In a single year, five records pointed jazz down five different roads: toward modes, odd meters, freedom from chords, harmonic speed and the church. All five are still argued about, and still played.

stops.note: Modes: instead of chords changing every bar or two, a whole section on one scale. Listen to how much room that leaves Miles, Coltrane and Cannonball.
What modal jazz means, and why it felt like a release after bebop's racing chords.
Odd meters: five and nine beats to the bar, played so smoothly that the record became a pop hit.
Freedom from chords: no piano, no fixed harmony, just melody and the players listening to one another. When the quartet opened at the Five Spot that November, musicians argued over it for weeks.
Harmonic speed: recorded in 1959, the title track moves through three keys every few bars. Coltrane runs every change at full speed; the pianist, Tommy Flanagan, barely gets through his solo.

stops.track: Charles Mingus|Better Git It in Your Soul
stops.note: The church: Mingus brings gospel shouts, hand claps and a revival-meeting energy into a jazz workshop band.

paths.outro: Each road has its own era in the app: Modal Jazz, Free Jazz, and Soul Jazz for the church. Pick one.

paths.title: Late Night
paths.subtitle: Ballads for after midnight
paths.intro: Slow music for the end of the evening. A ballad is where you hear what a player really sounds like: every note exposed, and the art in how long to hold it.

stops.note: The ballad that every saxophonist is measured against, improvised almost entirely away from the melody.
Holiday sings a wartime song of missing someone, slightly behind the beat, as if talking to herself.
Barely above a whisper, almost without vibrato.
Two chords repeated in the left hand for six minutes, and the right hand drifting free over them.

stops.ref: Duke Ellington & John Coltrane|In a Sentimental Mood|1962
stops.note: Ellington's piano introduction, then Coltrane's tenor at its calmest.
A baritone voice as deep as the hour, and Strayhorn's world-weary song.
Coltrane's ballad for his wife, over a held bass note.
A simple, folk-like melody with Jan Garbarek's saxophone, from Jarrett's European quartet.

paths.outro: For more slow music, the Songbook's ballads (Body and Soul, Lush Life, In a Sentimental Mood) each have several versions to compare.

paths.title: The Latin Tinge
paths.subtitle: Havana, New York and Rio in the music
paths.intro: Jelly Roll Morton said jazz needed a 'Spanish tinge'. From Afro-Cuban percussion in 1940s New York to bossa nova from Rio, Latin rhythm has run through jazz from the beginning.

stops.note: Where the son, the mambo and the rhythms behind Latin jazz came from.
The two-bar rhythmic key that everything in Afro-Cuban music lines up with.
Machito's Afro-Cubans, led musically by Mario Bauzá, mix big-band jazz with Cuban rhythm: Tanga is often called the first Latin jazz piece.
Gillespie's big band with the Cuban drummer Chano Pozo: bebop and Afro-Cuban percussion, at full strength.
The mambo at the Palladium: Tito Puente's band, built for dancers, with brass that swings as hard as any jazz band.
Bossa nova begins: João Gilberto's guitar and quiet voice, and a new, softer way to swing.
Mongo Santamaría takes a young Herbie Hancock's tune and turns it into a Latin pop hit.
Chucho Valdés returns to his early piano trio with batá drums, the sacred drums of Afro-Cuban religion.

paths.outro: The Latin Jazz & Bossa Nova era has the rest of the story, and Afro Blue in the Songbook shows a Latin tune becoming a jazz standard.

paths.title: One Tune, Five Decades
paths.subtitle: Body and Soul, from 1939 to now
paths.intro: Jazz is the art of playing the same song differently. Here is one song, a 1930 Broadway ballad, heard in four landmark versions. Listen for the bridge, the section where the chords move to a faraway key, and how each player gets through it.

stops.note: Where the song came from, and why it became a test piece.
Two choruses that leave the melody behind almost at once: a hit record made of pure improvisation.
The words Hawkins left out, sung as if confiding them.
Coltrane slows it down and adds his own moving chords underneath.
Solo piano: the melody stated plainly, then knocked off balance with Monk's dissonances.

paths.outro: The Songbook has 39 more tunes, each with versions across the decades.

paths.title: The Piano Trio
paths.subtitle: Three people, sixty years of rethinking it
paths.intro: Piano, bass and drums: the smallest jazz band that can do everything. Each of these trios changed what the other two players were for.

stops.note: Bebop piano: the right hand plays like a horn, the left drops sparse chords, and Max Roach's cowbell drives the Latin rhythm.
Ellington, Charles Mingus and Max Roach on Money Jungle: three leaders in one room, pushing each other hard.
Bill Evans, Scott LaFaro and Paul Motian, live in 1961: Gloria's Step is LaFaro's tune, and the bass is no longer just keeping time but a second melodic voice.
In a trio the comping, the chords behind a soloist, becomes a conversation.
Keith Jarrett, Gary Peacock and Jack DeJohnette take old standards and stretch them into long, singing improvisations.

stops.track: Brad Mehldau|Blame It on My Youth
stops.note: Mehldau's trio brings in counterpoint between the hands and, on later records, pop songs as standards.

paths.outro: The piano lineage traces where each of these pianists came from.

paths.title: From Hip-Hop Back to Jazz
paths.subtitle: The records the samples came from
paths.intro: From the late 1980s, hip-hop producers dug through old jazz records for loops, and their tracks sent listeners back to the originals. Each stop here is a jazz recording or tune that a hip-hop record was built on, and then the musicians who carried the conversation back the other way.

stops.note: Gang Starr's first single, Words I Manifest (1989), was built on a sample of Dizzy Gillespie's A Night in Tunisia. Play the versions here and listen for the bass vamp under the theme and the horn break before the solos.

A Tribe Called Quest's Jazz (We've Got) (1991) is built on an organ version of this tune by Jimmy McGriff, and the song's credits name Bronisław Kaper and Ned Washington, who wrote it for a 1947 film. Listen for the held bass note under its opening bars.

A Tribe Called Quest went further than sampling on the same album, The Low End Theory: they hired Ron Carter, Miles Davis's bassist in the 1960s, to play on Verses from the Abstract. Hear him here on Maiden Voyage, Footprints and Speak No Evil.

Us3, a London group given the run of the Blue Note archive, looped three one-bar pieces of this 1964 recording for Cantaloop (Flip Fantasia), which reached the US top ten. The same album built Eleven Long Years on Horace Silver's Song for My Father. Listen for the piano vamp, which barely changes for the whole track.
Madlib sampled this live Bill Evans Trio recording from Montreux for Raid, on the Madvillain album Madvillainy (2004). Listen for the minor-key theme Evans played for twenty years.

Kamasi Washington played tenor and arranged the strings on Kendrick Lamar's To Pimp a Butterfly, released in March 2015, with Robert Glasper on piano and keyboards. Two months later came Washington's own three-hour album, recorded years earlier with the same Los Angeles circle of musicians. Listen for the choir and strings around the band.

The method turned around: Makaya McCraven records bands improvising, in New York, Chicago, London and Los Angeles for this album, then cuts, layers and repitches the tapes the way a producer works with samples. He calls himself a beat scientist. Listen for loops you know were played live.

paths.outro: Every tune and recording on this path has more versions in the Songbook and more records on its artist's page. For jazz musicians and hip-hop in the same room, try Robert Glasper's Black Radio.

paths.title: The Protest Tradition
paths.subtitle: Songs that said something, and what they said it about
paths.intro: Jazz has always carried the history of the people who made it, and sometimes it named that history out loud: lynching, segregation, a church bombing, a prison uprising. Here are seven recordings, over seventy-five years, that each answered something in the news.

stops.note: Abel Meeropol's poem about lynching, sung by Billie Holiday in 1939. Columbia, her label, wouldn't record it for fear of Southern retailers and radio, so she made it for Milt Gabler's small Commodore label. Listen to how slowly she sings, holding back on every line.

A portrait of Orval Faubus, the Arkansas governor who in 1957 sent the National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock Central High School. Columbia wouldn't allow the words, so it's an instrumental here; Mingus recorded the version with lyrics for Candid in 1960. Listen for the mocking, lurching melody.

From We Insist! Max Roach's Freedom Now Suite (1960), begun for the centenary of the Emancipation Proclamation and hurried into the studio as the sit-ins spread. Abbey Lincoln sings Oscar Brown Jr.'s words about a slave overseer, then Coleman Hawkins solos. Listen to Lincoln alone at the start, keeping time on a tambourine.

Recorded in November 1963, two months after the Ku Klux Klan bombed the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham and killed four girls; it's widely heard as Coltrane's response. One account says the melody follows the rhythm of a speech by Martin Luther King. Listen to the saxophone phrase it like speech over McCoy Tyner's rolling chords.

Simone said she wrote it in under an hour, after the murder of Medgar Evers in Mississippi and the Birmingham bombing. It's built like a bright show tune; it was banned in several Southern states, and some radio stations sent their copies back broken in half. Listen to how cheerful the music stays while the words get angrier.
The title track of Shepp's 1972 album named for the Attica prison uprising of 1971: a band of more than thirty, with singers. Listen for the soul and funk in it, from a player known for free jazz.
Ambrose Akinmusire's Rollcall for Those Absent (2014) is a reading of the names of young people killed by gunfire, Trayvon Martin among them. Listen to each name in turn.

paths.outro: Christian Scott's K.K.P.D., inspired by an unwarranted traffic stop, and Archie Shepp's Malcolm, Malcolm – Semper Malcolm, on Fire Music, carry the tradition on; both are in the library.

paths.title: London Now
paths.subtitle: The scene around Nubya Garcia and Shabaka Hutchings
paths.intro: In the 2010s a generation of London musicians, many of them from community workshops, made the city one of jazz's liveliest scenes, mixing it with grime, Afrobeat and Caribbean music.

stops.note: Where it happened, and the workshops, Tomorrow's Warriors among them, where many of these players met.
Born in London and raised in Barbados, Hutchings came through Tomorrow's Warriors, led three bands at once and directed We Out Here (2018), the compilation that drew attention to the scene.

stops.ref: Sons of Kemet|In the Castle of My Skin
stops.note: Sons of Kemet was saxophone, tuba and two drummers, with no piano or guitar. Listen to the tuba play the bass line and the two drum kits lock into one Caribbean-inflected groove.

stops.ref: Shabaka Hutchings|My Queen Is Harriet Tubman
stops.note: From Your Queen Is a Reptile (2018), the band's first album for Impulse!, the label of John Coltrane's A Love Supreme. Listen to the tuba carry the whole bass line under the saxophone.

Nubya Garcia grew up in Camden with a Guyanese mother and a Trinidadian father, and also came through Tomorrow's Warriors. Her first album, Source (2020), was shortlisted for the Mercury Prize. Listen to her tenor sound, big and unhurried.

stops.ref: Nubya Garcia|La Cumbia Me Está Llamando
stops.note: Garcia with La Perla, an all-woman group from Colombia: a cumbia rhythm and their voices, with the saxophone weaving between them.

Hutchings stopped playing saxophone at the end of 2023, and his 2024 album is mostly flutes, from the Japanese shakuhachi to the Andean quena, recorded at Van Gelder Studio in New Jersey. On End of Innocence he plays clarinet with Jason Moran on piano. Listen to how quiet it is after Sons of Kemet.

paths.outro: For more cumbia and clave, try The Latin Tinge; for more flutes and slow, meditative jazz, the Spiritual Jazz era has Pharoah Sanders and Alice Coltrane.
